The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

content.description: The Markdown formatted text content to be written to the file.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.description: Executes a search query using the DuckDuckGo search engine and returns a specified number of search results from a given source. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

message.content:
Below you’ll find two ways to spin‑up a **Google Compute Engine** VM that has:

| Item | Details |
|------|---------|
| OS   | Ubuntu 20.04 LTS (`ubuntu-os-cloud/ubuntu-2004-focal-v20231102`) |
| GPU  | NVIDIA® RTX A6000 (24 GB) – one card per instance |
| Machine type | Custom “n1” family (you can tweak CPU/RAM if you wish) |

> ⚠️  
> *GCP does **not** have “EC2”; that’s Amazon Web Services.*  
> In GCP we talk about **Compute Engine** VMs.  

---

### 1️⃣ Quick CLI way – `gcloud`

```bash
PROJECT_ID="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-a"

# Create a custom n1 machine type with enough vCPU & RAM for your workload
MACHINE_TYPE="custom-8-32768"    # 8 vCPUs, 32 GiB memory

INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-demo"

# Image reference for Ubuntu 20.04 LTS
IMAGE_FAMILY="ubuntu-2004-lts"
IMAGE_PROJECT="ubuntu-os-cloud"

# Make sure the GPU quota exists first:
#   https://console.cloud.google.com/iam-admin/quota?q=GPU&filter=service%3Dcompute.googleapis.com

gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --zone="$ZONE" \
  --machine-type="$MACHINE_TYPE" \
  --subnet="default" \
  --network-tier="PREMIUM" \
  --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE \
  --provisioning-model=BASIC_PREEMPTIBLE \          # Optional: preemptible for cost savings
  --accelerator=count=1,type=nvidia-tesla-a100 \     # <-- change below!
  --boot-disk-size=50GB \
  --boot-disk-type=pd-standard \
  --image-family=$IMAGE_FAMILY \
  --image-project=$IMAGE_PROJECT \
  --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \   # optional init script
  --tags=http-server,https-server
```

#### Change the accelerator to **RTX A6000**

Replace the `--accelerator` flag above with:

```bash
--accelerator count=1,type=nvidia-tesla-a6000
```

So the full command becomes:

```bash
gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
  ... \
  --accelerator count=1,type=nvidia-tesla-a6000 \
  ...
```

> 👉 **Tip:**  
> - Verify that the zone supports the RTX A6000 (`gcloud compute zones describe $ZONE`).  
> - You might also add `--preemptibility=on` if you’re okay with interruptions but lower costs.

---

### 2️⃣ REST API approach

If you prefer programmatic creation via the Compute Engine REST API, here’s a minimal payload you’d POST to:

```
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/<PROJECT>/zones/<ZONE>/instances
```

```json
{
  "name": "<instance-name>",
  "machineType": "projects/<PROJECT>/zones/us-central1-a/machineTypes/custom-8-32768",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "diskSizeGb": 50,
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts"
      }
    }
  ],
  "labels": { },
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network":"global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs":[{"kind":"compute#accessConfig","type":"ONE_TO_ONE_NAT"}]
    }
  ],
  "scheduling": {
    "automaticRestart": false,
    "preemptible": true
  },
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/<PROJECT>/zones/us-central1-a/tags/nvidia-tesla-a6000"
    }
  ]
}
```

* Replace `<PROJECT>` and `<ZONE>` appropriately.  
* Ensure OAuth scopes allow `"https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"` so the API can provision GPUs.  
* After sending the request, poll the returned `operation` resource until its status is `"DONE"`.

---

### 🔧 Prerequisites Checklist

| Step | What to do |
|------|------------|
| 1 | Enable the **Compute Engine API** in your project. |
| 2 | Confirm you have sufficient **GPU quotas** for the target zone. |
| 3 | Install the latest `google-cloud-sdk` and run `gcloud auth login`. |
| 4 | Optionally set defaults: `gcloud config set project <PROJECT>` and `gcloud config set compute/region us-central1`, `gcloud config set compute/zones us-central1-a`. |
| 5 | Run either the CLI command or hit the REST endpoint. |

Once created, SSH into the instance (`gcloud compute ssh <instance-name>`) and install CUDA drivers if you plan to run GPU workloads beyond what comes preinstalled with the base image.

Happy hacking! 🚀
